title: How to Use First-Party Data to Drive Sales During Peak Events
summary: Learn how to use first-party data, CRM segmentation and automation to drive stronger engagement and revenue during Black Friday, EOFY and other peak sales events.
body_markdown:
Black Friday. Cyber Monday. Boxing Day. Christmas.


[Every mega sales event](http://au.pattern.com/blog/2026-key-sales-events/) promises the same thing: a flood of traffic, a spike in orders, and a painfully short window to get it right. Most brands respond the same way. They discount harder and spend more on ads. But your most valuable resource isn’t a bigger media budget. It’s the first-party data you already have on the customers who know your brand best


## **Why first-party data matters more when the pressure’s on**


During mega sales events, every brand in your category bids for the same cold traffic at once,


[so acquisition costs spike](http://au.pattern.com/blog/using-ai-in-advertising-during-peak-season/) . The data you already own sits ready to use instead: purchase history, browsing behavior, email and SMS engagement, loyalty status, and preference-centre answers. While competitors overpay for strangers, you go straight to the people most likely to buy.


That data typically includes:


- Purchase history and average order value


- Browsing and product-view behavior


- Email and SMS engagement scores


- Loyalty tier or VIP status


- Preference-centre or quiz responses


**The Australian calendar makes this harder, not easier.** Australian brands do not get one peak. They get a run of them, and several land close enough together that there’s no time to rebuild an audience in between. Click Frenzy runs several editions through the year with the main event in November. Black Friday falls on 27 November 2026, Cyber Monday on 30 November, and Boxing Day on 26 December. That puts three major events inside five weeks.


The compression is the argument for owned data. A brand leaning on paid acquisition has to win the same auction four or five times a year, at exactly the moments every competitor is bidding. A brand with clean segments and working flows sends to the same owned audience each time and only has to change the offer.


It also means the same contacts hear from you repeatedly across a short window. Fatigue compounds across events, not just within one. Someone who was hit hard through Cyber Week is a different prospect on 26 December than they were in October, and your segmentation should reflect that.


## **Five ways to put first-party data to work**


### 1. Make sure your data is actually connected


First-party data is only valuable if you can use it. Customer information often sits across ecommerce, ESP, loyalty, SMS and onsite platforms, so make sure key signals are flowing into your CRM and can support segmentation, personalisation and automation.


The goal is not to collect more data. It is to make the data you already have actionable.


### 2. Segment before the sale starts


Don’t wait until launch day to figure out who gets what. Build your segments in the weeks before the event, so every send has a clear audience from minute one. As Klaviyo’s own


[BFCM email marketing strategy guide](https://www.klaviyo.com/bfcm/email-marketing-strategy) puts it, the more precise your segments, the more relevant and effective your messaging can be.


- Give VIP and high-LTV customers early access, before the general list


- Build a dedicated win-back segment for lapsed customers with a distinct offer


- Separate high-AOV shoppers from deal-hunters so each gets a relevant message


### 3. Personalize the offer, not just the subject line


Not every customer requires the same incentive. Blanket-discounting erodes margin for nothing. Use purchase history to recommend what they’ll actually want instead.


- Cross-sell bundles based on past purchase categories


- Tier offers by engagement or spend level, rather than sending one flat percentage to everyone


- Exclude recent full-price buyers from your deepest discounts


### 4. Let engagement data set your send cadence


Sending everyone the same run of emails across a five-day sale is a fast way to tank deliverability. Engagement data should decide who hears from you more, who hears less, and who moves to another channel entirely. Dotdigital’s


[2026 Black Friday and Cyber Monday data](https://dotdigital.com/blog/black-friday-cyber-monday-stats/) flags the same risk, warning that blasting irrelevant offers to an entire list drives “BFCM fatigue” and pushes subscribers to disengage.


- Throttle frequency for low-engagement segments


- Prioritise SMS for high-intent shoppers who’ve engaged recently


- Hold your least-engaged contacts back from peak-frequency sends altogether


Peak volume also exposes anything broken underneath. If consent filters or suppression rules are not set correctly, a sale week is when it surfaces, and


[the compliance gaps sitting in most CRM setups](http://au.pattern.com/blog/the-hidden-crm-compliance-gaps/?utm_source=peak-events-first-party-data) are worth checking before you scale sends.


### 5. Capture the moment for what comes after


Mega sales events bring a wave of net-new customers. What you collect from them now shapes how well you retain them later.


- Capture preferences (category interest, birthday)


- Tune abandoned cart and browse flows to reflect the promotion they saw


- Trigger a welcome series built from sale-specific data, not a generic template


## **Smarter CRM drives revenue growth**


For one ecommerce client, a targeted BFCM CRM strategy generated


**$1.13M in CRM-attributed revenue, up 69% YoY** , despite a shorter campaign window.


Rather than increasing send volume, the strategy used behavioural and engagement data to reduce email fatigue, reach high-intent customers via SMS, shorten browse and cart abandonment delays, and align flows with sale-specific messaging.


The result was stronger peak performance without relying on more sends or deeper discounts.


## **Is your CRM making enough of your first-party data?**


Most established brands already have valuable customer data. The bigger question is whether their CRM setup is actually using it.


Segmentation may be too broad. Key behavioural flows may be missing. Valuable data could be sitting in Shopify, a loyalty platform or your ESP without influencing communications. And without a buttoned-up view of


[how channels perform together](http://au.pattern.com/blog/why-sem-and-seo-should-be-measured-together/?utm_source=peak-first-party-data) , it is hard to see what data is worth.


A CRM audit can uncover these gaps before they become missed revenue opportunities.

# Frequently Asked Questions


What is first-party data in CRM?


**


**


First-party data is information a brand collects directly from its customers and audiences, including purchase history, website behaviour, email and SMS engagement, loyalty activity and preferences.


How can first-party data improve Black Friday email marketing?


**


**


It lets brands segment customers by value, intent, interests and previous behaviour, then tailor offers, products, timing and messaging instead of sending the same promotion to everyone.


What first-party data should ecommerce brands collect?


**


**


Prioritise data you can use. Purchase history, product interest, engagement, customer value and lifecycle stage are often the most actionable. Preferences, birthday and location can also support useful segmentation and personalisation.


Is first-party data compliant under the Privacy Act?


**


**


Collecting and using first-party data is generally compliant under Australia’s Privacy Act 1988, provided brands meet their obligations under the Australian Privacy Principles – collecting only what’s needed, being transparent about how it’s used, and giving customers a clear way to opt out of marketing.


What's the difference between first-party and third-party data?


**


**


First-party data is what you collect directly from your own customers and channels, including purchase history, on-site behaviour, and email or SMS engagement. Third-party data is bought or aggregated from external providers with no direct relationship to your brand. First-party data tends to be more accurate and relevant, since it comes straight from people who already know you.


Are there specific Australian sales events brands should plan their CRM around?


**


**


Yes. Beyond global moments like Black Friday and Cyber Monday, Australian brands typically plan around EOFY sales in June, Afterpay Day in March and August, Click Frenzy in May and October, and Boxing Day from 26 December. Building segments and flows around this local calendar, not just the US retail calendar, is one of the biggest gaps we see when auditing CRM programs.
